title: The Crop App That Missed Cassava

pages.text: At a women’s gari-processing cooperative near Assin Foso, Mawuli’s aunties knew that good gari starts with sound cassava roots and careful processing: hygienic peeling, washing, grating, controlled fermentation and pressing to help reduce naturally occurring cyanogenic compounds, sieving, and thorough roasting. Fortification, if used, requires a separately approved and measured ingredient process. When Afia tested a downloaded “Smart Farm AI” leaf-camera app on mottled yellow-and-green cassava leaves showing symptoms consistent with cassava mosaic disease, the app confidently flashed: “96% Match: Maple Leaf Frostbite: Apply Winter Mulch!” Bature burst out laughing: “Snow frostbite in Ghana? Why did a smart computer say something so foolish?”

pages.alt: Beside a Ghanaian cassava farm, Afia holds a tablet showing a mottled leaf mislabelled as Maple Frostbite while Bature and Mawuli look on amazed.

pages.text: In Computing class, Madam Adomako turned that funny mistake into a vital lesson on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). “AI does not ‘think’ like a human elder,” she explained. “In supervised Machine Learning, an algorithm learns patterns solely from thousands of labelled examples called training data. The app’s sample documentation showed mostly temperate crops and very few examples of tropical cassava, plantain, or cocoyam. We cannot know its complete training data without the developer’s records. This is an example of how unrepresentative training data can contribute to algorithmic bias or unreliable predictions; a high confidence score does not prove a diagnosis.”

pages.text: With farmers’ permission and an Agricultural Extension Officer checking the disease labels, the JHS club collected a deliberately varied teaching dataset of 180 cassava leaf photographs across different farms and lighting conditions. This improved coverage but did not guarantee a representative sample! Bature recorded the verified tally cleanly in a frequency table: Healthy Leaves = 90; Suspected Cassava Mosaic Disease = 45; Green Mite Damage = 27; and Suspected Bacterial Blight = 18 (Total = 180 photographed leaves).

Bature recorded the verified tally cleanly in a frequency table: Healthy Leaves = 90; Suspected Cassava Mosaic Disease = 45; Green Mite Damage = 27; and Suspected Bacterial Blight = 18 (Total = 180 photographed leaves).
pages.alt: Afia, Bature, and Mawuli photographing cassava leaves in varied lighting with an extension officer, recording tallies totaling 180 verified samples.

pages.text: To present the dataset distribution to the cooperative, Bature constructed an accurate pie chart in his Mathematics book, avoiding the common mistake of plotting raw numbers or percentages directly as degrees! “A full circle measures 360°,” Bature reminded Mawuli. “Each sector angle equals (Category Frequency ÷ Total Frequency) × 360°.” Calculating carefully: Healthy = (90 ÷ 180) × 360° = 180°; Mosaic Disease = (45 ÷ 180) × 360° = 90°; Green Mite = (27 ÷ 180) × 360° = 54°; and Bacterial Blight = (18 ÷ 180) × 360° = 36°. Checking the sum, 180° + 90° + 54° + 36° = 360°, every degree was accounted for!

pages.text: Using a classroom image classifier in the ICT lab, Afia grouped photographs by source plant before splitting them, to reduce the chance that near-identical photos appeared in both sets. The group trained on 144 photos and reserved 36 unseen photos for a small demonstration test. On that test, their model classified 33 of 36 correctly (91.7%, about 92%). They had not run a comparable test of the downloaded app, so they did not claim a proven improvement over it! Even then, Madam Adomako taught a crucial ethical rule: “Three of these 36 test images were misclassified, and performance on other farms or in different light remains unknown. Responsible AI keeps a ‘human-in-the-loop’, where farmers and extension officers verify high-stakes decisions rather than obeying software blindly, and farmer farm-location privacy must always be respected.”

pages.text: At Friday’s cooperative meeting, the students presented their colour-coded pie chart alongside a laminated visual leaf guide and their locally trained offline classifier, helping farmers recognise possible disease symptoms and consult extension officers about removing affected plants and choosing healthy, recommended planting material. Months later, harvesting sound tubers for Mawuli’s aunties to roast into golden soya-fortified gari in hygienic stainless-steel pans, the trio saw how African data, honest statistics, and food technology make Artificial Intelligence truly serve local communities.

activities.question: Why did the downloaded "Smart Farm AI" app misclassify Cassava Mosaic as "Maple Frostbite"?
options: Model suffered training bias because tropical crops were missing
Snow falls nightly across Central Region cassava farms in July
Smartphone cameras cannot photograph green chlorophyll near the Equator

activities.question: In a survey of 180 cassava plants, 45 plants had Mosaic Virus. What sector angle represents this on a pie chart?
options: 45°, because frequency is plotted directly as degrees

activities.question: In Career Technology, why must grated cassava mash undergo fermentation, pressing, and roasting during gari making?
options: To break down toxic cyanogenic compounds safely and reduce moisture
To add wet mud and increase bacterial spoilage inside storage bags
To turn fibrous cassava peelings into raw unseasoned timber

activities.prompt: Put the ethical Machine Learning and statistical workflow in the correct scientific order.
items: Collect diverse, expert-verified leaf images across varied lighting.
Tabulate frequencies and calculate exact 360° pie-chart sector angles.
Train classifier on training split while holding back separate test set.
Evaluate accuracy on unseen leaves with human-in-the-loop check.
